=== Kurozumikyō ===
{{Main|Kurozumikyō}}
Kurozumikyō (黒住教) is a group highly linked to [[Amaterasu]].

=== Shinto Shusei ===
{{nihongo|Shinto Shusei|神道修成派}} is considered a form of [[Confucian Shinto]].{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=5-6}}<ref name="caroline-myss-2023a">{{Cite web |title=The Forms of Shinto |url=https://www.myss.com/free-resources/world-religions/shinto/the-forms-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-03-06 |website=Caroline Myss |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" /> It was founded in 1849 by {{ill|Nitta Kuniteru|en|Nitta Kuniteru|WD=Q123561044|lt=Nitta Kuniteru}} (1829–1902),<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> who was known to have read the {{ill|Analects|en|Analects|WD=Q276015|lt=Analects}} at age 9.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> He founded the sect at age twenty,<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> and considered Japanese people to be descendants of deities.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> He considered allegiance to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan}} to be central to his philosophy; he was a supporter of [[Sonnō jōi]] but supported the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin Rebellion}} and the [[Meiji Restoration]] later.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" />

Alongside [[Kurozumikyō]], it was one of the first two Shinto sects to gain independence in 1876.<ref name="戦後に神社本庁を形成する前身組織の1つ-2" /> It has not been very active in the postwar era.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2001 |title=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms - Shintô shûsei-ha 神道修成派 |url=https://archive.today/20230321180610/https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_S.html |publisher=Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics, Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

=== Jingūkyō ===
{{Main|Jingūkyō}}
{{Nihongo|Jingūkyō|神宮教}} was a sect run out of [[Ise Grand Shrine]] which distributed [[Jingū taima|Jingu Taima]]. It was a rival to [[Izumo-taishakyo]] and eventually left the federation and came to dominate {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}}.

=== Izumo-taishakyo ===
{{Main|Izumo-taishakyo}}
Izumo-taishakyo was founded by [[Senge Takatomi]].<ref name="google3"/><ref>{{cite book |author1=Teeuwen, M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yBFFAz4z3gUC |title=Shinto, a Short History |author2=Breen, J. |author3=Inoue, N. |author4=Mori, M. |date=2003 |publisher=RoutledgeCurzon |isbn=9780415311793 |page=177 |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref>  and has 1,266,058 followers.<ref name="Religious Almanac" /> It is a [[Fukko Shinto]] lineage and at one point was a major rival with [[Jingūkyō]].

=== Fuso-kyo ===
{{nihongo|Fusō-kyō|扶桑教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship}} sect traditionally seen to have been founded by {{ill|Hasegawa Kakugyo|en|Hasegawa Kakugyo|WD=Q11630860|lt=Hasegawa Kakugyo}} (who was also associated with Jikkō kyō).<ref name="picken-2010a">{{Cite book |last=Picken |first=Stuart D. B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=Jikk%C5%8D+ky%C5%8D&pg=PA131 |title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto |date=2010-12-28 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Jikkō kyō ===
{{nihongo|Jikkō kyō|実行教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship}} sect traditionally seen to have been founded by {{ill|Hasegawa Kakugyo|en|Hasegawa Kakugyo|WD=Q11630860|lt=Hasegawa Kakugyo}} (who was also associated with Fusō-kyō).<ref name="picken-2010a" />

=== Shinto Taiseikyo ===
{{Main|Shinto Taiseikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Shinto Taiseikyo|神道大成教}} is a [[Confucian Shinto]] sect<ref name="caroline-myss-2023a"/><ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" /> founded by {{ill|Hirayama Seisai|en|Hirayama Seisai|WD=Q24874598|lt=Hirayama Seisai}}.

=== Shinshu-kyo ===
{{Nihongo|Shinshu-kyo|神習教}} is a "purification sect" alongside [[Misogikyo]].<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

It was founded by Masaki Yoshimura<ref>{{Cite web |last=小項目事典 |first=朝日日本歴史人物事典,デジタル版 日本人名大辞典+Plus,ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 |title=芳村正秉(よしむら・まさもち)とは？ 意味や使い方 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%8A%B3%E6%9D%91%E6%AD%A3%E7%A7%89-146230 |access-date=2023-03-06 |website=コトバンク |language=ja}}</ref> (1839–1915<ref>{{Cite web |title=歴史 |url=http://shinshukyo.jp/%e6%ad%b4%e5%8f%b2/ |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=神道神習教公式ページ |language=ja}}</ref>), who was a survivor of the {{ill|Ansei Purge|en|Ansei Purge|WD=Q569487|lt=Ansei Purge}}.{{sfn|井上順孝|1991|p=277-278}} He worked at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]] and later was head of [[Tatsuta Taisha|Tatsuta Shrine]], but due to laws restricting teaching, he entrusted his children to [[Itō Hirobumi]] (before he became Prime Minister) and established a new branch based on his {{ill|family knowledge|ja|家学|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/family knowledge|qq=}}.{{sfn|井上順孝|1991|p=282}}

=== Ontake-kyo ===
{{Main|Ontake-kyo}}
{{Nihongo|Ontake-kyo|御嶽教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship}} sect dedicated to {{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake|WD=Q1754806|lt=Mount Ontake}}.<ref>{{cite book |author=Holtom, D.C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=znzXAAAAMAAJ |title=The National Faith of Japan: A Study in Modern Shinto |date=1938 |publisher=Paragon Book Reprint Corporation |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> It had 3 million members in 1930,<ref name="googlebooks">{{cite book |author=Picken, S.D.B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yA3_11C6pPgC |title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings |date=1994 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=9780313264313 |page=232 |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> which decreased to around 40,000 members in 2020.<ref name="Religious Almanac" />

=== Shinto Taikyo ===
{{Main|Shinto Taikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Shintō Taikyō|神道大教}} is the direct successor to the [[Taikyo Institute]]. Its name "Taikyo" refers to the [[:en:Three Great Teachings|Three Great Teachings]] first proclaimed in the [[Taikyo Proclamation|Proclamation of the Great Doctrine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shinto Taikyo |url=http://www.philtar.ac.uk/encyclopedia/shinto/shitai.html |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.philtar.ac.uk}}</ref>

=== Shinrikyo ===
{{nihongo|Shinrikyo|神理教|4={{lit|divine principle}}}} is a Shinto sect considered to be part of the [[Fukko Shinto]] lineage of Sect Shinto, alongside [[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinto Taikyo]] and [[Izumo-taishakyo]].{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=5-6}} The name "Shinrikyo" is relatively common among Shinto groups,<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> and uses different {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji}} characters than {{ill|Aum Shinrikyo|en|Aum Shinrikyo|WD=Q217408|lt=Aum Shinrikyo}}, a cult and terrorist organization.

It was founded by {{ill|Tsunehiko Sano|ja|佐野経彦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunehiko Sano|1=Tsunehiko Sano|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11385093}}<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp">{{Cite web |title=Sano Tsunehiko and "Divine Principle (Shinri)" |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/cpjr/kami/inoue.html |access-date=2023-03-05 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref><ref name="日本国語大辞典,百科事典マイペディア,デジタル大辞泉,世界大百科事典内言及" /> in 1880.<ref name="notes-1989a" /><ref name="日本国語大辞典,百科事典マイペディア,デジタル大辞泉,世界大百科事典内言及" /> Sano had previously studied medicine and was an advocate of traditional Japanese medicine. He studied {{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku}} in his youth under Nishida Naokai.<ref>https://rks.accesson.kr/assets/pdf/2564/journal-23-1-211.pdf {{Bare URL PDF|date=August 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp//eos/detail/id=9473|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム}}</ref>

Sano's thought blurred the lines between monotheism and polytheism, entering {{ill|Transtheism|en|Transtheism|WD=Q312221|lt=Transtheism}}.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> His concept of {{Transl|ja|[[kami]]}} was aimed at resisting the propagation of Christianity while composing teachings that were in line with the aims of popular national indoctrination. His core elements of the concept of {{Transl|ja|kami}} did not change throughout his life.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" />

He believed the etymology of {{Transl|ja|kami}} was derived from {{Nihongo|vital force||Ikimochi}}. He saw this as emphasizing the interconnectedness of everything, from humans to nature, and as such this could be interpreted as a monotheistic view.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> He saw all the {{Transl|ja|kami}} as unified under a divine principle, hence the name of the group.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" />

=== Misogikyo ===
{{nihongo|Misogikyo|禊教|4={{lit|[[Misogi]] religion}}}} is considered a "purification sect" alongside [[Shinshu-kyo]].<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

The group is quite obscure today.<ref name="sawada-1998a">{{Cite journal |last=Sawada |first=Janine Anderson |date=1998 |title=Mind and Morality in Nineteenth-Century Japanese Religions: Misogi-Kyō and Maruyama-Kyō |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1399927 |journal=Philosophy East and West |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=108–141 |doi=10.2307/1399927 |jstor=1399927 |issn=0031-8221}}</ref> It is very ritual-focused, with little theoretical theology. In this way, it contrasts with [[:en:Yoshida Shinto|Yoshida Shinto]].<ref name="sawada-1998a" /> It emphasizes right state of mind and self-control.<ref name="sawada-1998a" /> It has influence from [[Confucian Shinto]] but is its own tradition.<ref name="sawada-1998a" />

=== Konkokyo ===
{{Main|Konkokyo}}
{{Nihongo|Konkōkyō|金光教|Konkō-kyō}} is a group often considered to be its own religion, which emerged from [[Shinbutsu-shūgō]].

=== Tenrikyo ===
{{Main|Tenrikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Tenrikyo||Tenrikyō|sometimes rendered as 'Tenriism'}} is a Sect Shinto group founded by {{ill|Nakayama Miki|en|Nakayama Miki|WD=Q2723199|lt=Nakayama Miki}}. It is often considered a separate religion from Shinto.

=== Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto ===
{{Main|Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto}}
In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the Tsuchimikado family, descendants of [[Abe no Seimei]], established [[Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto]] influenced by [[Confucian Shinto]] through [[Suika Shinto]]. However, because of the inclusion of fortune-telling and magic, the Meiji government considered it pagan and issued the {{interlanguage link|Tensha Shinto Prohibition Ordinance|ja|天社禁止令|1=Tensha Shinto Prohibition Ordinance}}. After the war, it was restored as "Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto Headquarters", and registered as a [[religious corporation]] rather than a Sect Shinto or a Shinto shrine.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

=== Oomoto ===
{{Main|Oomoto}}
{{Nihongo|Oomoto|大本|Ōmoto|{{lit|Great Source, or Great Origin}}}} is often seen as a new religion.

=== New Sect Shinto ===
{{See also|Japanese new religions}}
{{Nihongo|New Sect Shinto||shin kyoha Shinto}}<ref name="google2">{{cite book|title=Excel Senior High School Studies of Religion|author=Fleming, L.|date=2001|publisher=Pascal Press |isbn=9781740202411 |url={{Google books |plainurl=yes |id=Q_K81HQFoyoC }} |page=278|access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> is a subset of Sect Shinto,<ref name="jinja">{{cite web|url=http://jinja.jp/english/s-2.html|title=Shuha Shinto|publisher=jinja.jp|access-date=2015-01-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150101161525/http://jinja.jp/english/s-2.html|archive-date=2015-01-01|url-status=dead}}</ref> and consists of numerous organizations.<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=World Christian Trends, AD 30-AD 2200: Interpreting the Annual Christian Megacensus|author1=Barrett, D.B.|author2=Johnson, T.M.|author3=Guidry, C.R.|author4=Crossing, P.F.|date=2001|issue=Bd. 1|publisher=William Carey Library|isbn=9780878086085 |url={{Google books |plainurl=yes |id=IMRsJ1gnIYkC }} |page=606|access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> It is influenced by {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} and {{ill|Confucianism|en|Confucianism|WD=Q9581|lt=Confucianism}}.<ref name="jinja" />

It is part of the Sect Shinto movement not centering upon 13 sects.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003">{{cite journal | citeseerx=10.1.1.567.8041 | title=Intercultural Communication Studies XII-4 2003 Asian Approaches to Human Communication Aspects of Shinto in Japanese Communication }}</ref> New Shinto sects have {{ill|Shamanism|en|Shamanism|WD=Q42042|lt=shamanistic}} leadership, syncretism of religious and philosophical beliefs, closely knit social organization, and individualism.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003"/> Some groups have characteristics of {{ill|Monotheism|en|Monotheism|WD=Q9159|lt=Monotheism}}, in the extreme case making a compromise of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}, {{ill|Confucianism|en|Confucianism|WD=Q9581|lt=Confucianism}}, and {{ill|Folk religion|en|Folk religion|WD=Q1068640|lt=Folk religion}}.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003"/>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sekten-Shintō]][[en:Sect Shinto]][[fr:Sectes Shinto]][[id:Sekte Shinto]][[ja:教派神道]][[ko:교파신토]][[lv:Sektu sintoisms]][[pl:Shintō sekciarskie]][[ru:Кёха синто]][[simple:Sect Shinto]][[zh:教派神道]]

{{Short description|Non-mainstream Shinto sects}}
{{nihongo|'''Sect Shinto'''|教派神道|Kyōha Shintō|or 宗派, {{transl|ja|Shuha Shintō}}}} refers to several independent organized [[Shinto]] groups that were excluded by {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Japanese|1=Empire of Japan}} law in 1882 from government-run {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}.<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica">{{Cite web |date=July 20, 1998 |title=Kyōha Shintō |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kyoha-Shinto |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=Britannica |language=en}}</ref> These independent groups have more developed {{ill|Theology|en|Theology|WD=Q34178|lt=Theology|1=Theology}} than mainstream [[Shrine Shinto]], which focuses more on rituals.<ref>[[景山春樹]] 「神道」『世界大百科事典』 219頁。</ref> Many such groups are organized into the {{Nihongo|Association of Sectarian Shinto|教派神道連合会|Kyōha Shintō Rengōkai}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=教派神道連合会（教派連） |url=http://kyoharen.jp/ |access-date=2018-12-23 |publisher=Kyoharen.jp}}</ref> Before World War II, Sect Shinto consisted of 13 denominations, which were referred to as the 13 Shinto schools. Since then, there have been additions and withdrawals of membership.

Whereas Shrine Shinto is an aggregation of various shrines and customary beliefs in various parts of Japan (which became united under the [[Ise Grand Shrine]] after the Meiji period), Sect Shinto is based on the {{Transl|ja|{{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku|1=Kokugaku}}}} ({{Lit|national study}}) school of philosophy. [[Tenrikyo]] was categorized as Sect Shinto but is often considered a separate {{ill|God|en|God|WD=Q190|lt=monotheistic|1=God}} religion.<ref>Fukaya, Tadamasa, "The Fundamental Doctrines of Tenrikyo," Tenrikyo Overseas Mission Department, Tenri-Jihosha, 1960, p.2</ref>

== Overview ==
While it has roots in the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, Sect Shinto became more firmly established in the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} after the [[Meiji Restoration]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Bowker |first=John |title=Kyōha Shintō |date=2003-01-01 |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780192800947.001.0001/acref-9780192800947-e-4172 |work=The Concise Oxford Dictionary of World Religions |access-date=2022-04-30 |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/acref/9780192800947.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-280094-7}}</ref> Its formation was stimulated by the religious policies of the Meiji government,<ref name="nobutaka-2023a">{{Cite web |last=Nobutaka |first=Inoue |title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - 8. Schools, Groups, and Personalities |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp//eos/detail/id=9919 |access-date=2023-05-16 |website= |publisher={{ill|Kokugakuin University|en|Kokugakuin University|WD=Q495330|lt=Kokugakuin University|1=Kokugakuin University}} |language=}}</ref> and it emerged at a time when there was increasing theological discussion among people of a wider range of classes, rather than only between intellectuals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Perspectives toward Understanding the Concept of Kami |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/cpjr/kami/intro.html |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref>

In 1868, the religious administration of the new Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto-Buddhist Separation Order]], resulting in the {{Transl|ja|[[haibutsu kishaku]]}} and the restoration of the [[:en:Unity of ritual and government|Unity of ritual and government]] system. Following the [[Taikyo Proclamation]], which designated Shinto as the state religion, the [[Taikyo Institute|Great Teaching Institute]] was established, though it was soon reformed into the [[Bureau of Shinto Affairs]] and later the sect [[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinto Taikyo]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}}

During these early trial-and-error religious policies, the Meiji government promoted a nationalized system of Shinto education by religious instructors known as {{Transl|ja|[[Kyodo Shoku|kyōdō shoku]]}}.<ref name="nobutaka-2023a" /> However, with the spread of the ideas of {{ill|Separation of church and state|en|Separation of church and state|WD=Q753623|lt=Separation of church and state|1=Separation of church and state}} and {{ill|Freedom of religion|en|Freedom of religion|WD=Q171899|lt=Freedom of religion|1=Freedom of religion}}, the {{Transl|ja|kyōdō shoku}} ended. This produced a division in Shinto between shrines for state-run public rituals and religious groups centered on edification.<ref name="nobutaka-2023a" /> Groups that met certain conditions (such as the number of followers) were officially recognized as "independent denominations." This was the beginning of the denominational Sect Shinto.

This separation strengthened the idea that it was necessary to establish an institution that was a more developed version of the former Shodo Shido Practice Center.{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}} Accordingly, the Meiji government established the [[:en:Office of Japanese Classics Research|Office of Japanese Classics Research]] in Tokyo Prefecture, independent of the Bureau of Shinto Affairs, in order to organize the exploration of ideas unique to Japan. It was later succeeded by {{ill|Kokugakuin University|en|Kokugakuin University|WD=Q495330|lt=Kokugakuin University|1=Kokugakuin University}}.

== Establishment ==
=== Formation of a united government ===
The impetus for denominational Shinto was the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, which began in 1868 (first year of Meiji) with the revival of the [[Department of Divinities]] and the [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Shinto and Buddhism]], which started with the Shinto-Buddhist Hanzen Order, a [[Daijō-kan|premodern imperial government]] directive.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=18-19}} This led to the formation of the [[:en:Unity of religion and rule|unity of ritual and government]], and a Shinto government was revived. Around then, official decrees abolished the hereditary system of Shinto priests, thus ending the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Shirakawa family|lt=Shirakawa|ja|白川伯王家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa family|qq=}} and {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|lt=Yoshida families|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|qq=}} over Shinto.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=18-19}}{{Quote frame|The rituals of the Shinto shrines are the religious services of the state, and it is, of course, true that they are not the private property of one person or one family. This is a common practice in the country, and priests are considered to be a separate species from the people.| Meiji 4th Year Taishogun's Bulletin No. 234}}During this transition, the concept of missionaries to propagate Shinto remained. In 1870 (Meiji 3), the imperial [[Taikyo Proclamation]] designated Shinto as the state religion.<ref name="仏教辞典2版2">{{Cite book |last=中村元ほか編 |title=岩波仏教辞典 |publisher=岩波書店 |year=2002 |isbn=978-4000802055 |edition=第二版 |pages=220–222}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms: T |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_T.html#taikyo_sempu |access-date=2023-03-10 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref> The [[Taikyo Institute|Great Teaching Institute]] was established in 1872 (Meiji 5) as a missionary organization, but was dissolved in 1875 (Meiji 8). It was succeeded by the [[Bureau of Shinto Affairs]] in the same year, to which the originally disparate folk belief religions belonged.

=== Ministry of Religion, {{Transl|ja|kyōdō shoku}}, and the Taikyo Institute ===
In 1872, the [[Missionary Office]] was abolished and replaced with the [[Ministry of Religion (Japan)|Ministry of Religion]].{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=20}} In April, Shinto priests and monks were assigned {{Transl|ja|[[Kyodo Shoku|kyōdō shoku]]}} positions, of which there were 14 Ranks.<ref name="仏教辞典2版2" /> The Ministry was later dissolved in 1877, and {{Transl|ja|kyōdō shoku}} was abolished in 1884.{{Sfn|村上|1974|pp=118-119}}

The priesthood was initially divided in two geographically in two, with the eastern division headed by {{ill|Konoe Tadafusa|en|Konoe Tadafusa|WD=Q3198724|lt=Konoe Tadafusa|1=Konoe Tadafusa}}, priest of [[Ise Grand Shrine]], and the western division headed by [[Senge Takatomi]], the grand priest of [[Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha Shrine]]. Since it was assumed that one's religious affiliation was free, there was a struggle for power between the Ise and Izumo factions.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=25-26,35}} On January 30, 1873, the two-part system was abolished and the two regions were combined. However, they were once again divided later{{When|date=May 2023}} becoming a three-part system with [[Senge Takatomi]], {{ill|Koga Takemichi|ja|%E4%B9%85%E6%88%91%E5%BB%BA%E9%80%9A|1=Koga Takemichi|2=ja|3=久我建通|WD=Q7138768|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koga Takemichi|qq=}}, and {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|en|Inaba Masakuni|WD=Q6013270|lt=Inaba Masakuni|1=Inaba Masakuni}}, and then a four-part system with the addition of Tanaka Yoriyasu, the grand priest of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]]. On that same day,{{When|date=May 2023}} the [[Kurozumikyō]] and {{ill|Shinto Shusei|en|Shinto Shusei|WD=Q11590921|lt=Shinto Shusei|1=Shintō Shūsei-ha}} were specially established as denominational Shinto sects, and the compartment system was abolished.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=25-26}}

In May 1873, the Ministry of Religion issued a religious  ordinance, which set standards for the approval of {{Transl|ja|[[:en:Kosha (lecture group)|kosha]]}} (religious lectures or meetings). In August, the Ministry approved the Kurozumikyō, the Tohokami (later [[Misogikyo|Misogi-Kyo]]), the Mitake, and the Fuji Isan (later [[Fuso-kyo]]), as well as Buddhist {{Transl|ja|kosha}}.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=94}}

In 1873, the [[Taikyo Institute|Great Teaching Institute]] was established—first in Kojimachi, {{ill|Kioichō, Chiyoda, Tokyo|en|Kioichō, Chiyoda, Tokyo|WD=Q3347243|lt=Kioicho|1=Kioichō, Chiyoda, Tokyo}} and later in Masukami, Shiba at {{ill|Zōjō-ji|en|Zōjō-ji|WD=Q249139|lt=Zōjō-ji|1=Zōjō-ji}}—as the head temple for {{Transl|ja|kyōdō shoku}} of a joint Shinto and Buddhist sect.{{Sfn|菅田|1985|pp=113-114}} The Taikyo Institute was initiated by the Buddhist side to concretize teaching by the Ministry of Religion, but it later became focused entirely on Shinto.{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=21}} The Buddhist side, led by [[Jōdo Shinshū|Shinshū]], broke away from the institute.{{Sfn|菅田|1985|pp=113-114}} On April 30, 1875, the Taikyo Institute was dissolved by order of the Ministry of Religion.{{Sfn|村上|2007|pp=103-104}}

=== Bureau of Shinto Affairs ===
The [[Bureau of Shinto Affairs]] was formed in March 1875, just prior to the dissolution of the Taikyo Institute, by a group of Shinto shrines,  at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] and other shrines throughout Japan, as well as by Shinto priests and instructors belonging to private Shinto-related {{Transl|ja|[[:en:Kosha (lecture group)|kosha]]}}.{{Sfn|菅田|1985|pp=113-114}} The Shinto side felt that there was no organization that corresponded to the various Buddhist sects,{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=21}} and on March 27, 1875 (Meiji 8), Grand High Priest Suechi Sanjonishi, Grand Priest-in-Charge {{ill|Inaba Masakuni|en|Inaba Masakuni|WD=Q6013270|lt=Inaba Masakuni|1=Inaba Masakuni}}, Yoriyasu Tanaka, {{ill|Hirayama Seisai|en|Hirayama Seisai|WD=Q24874598|lt=Hirayama Seisai|1=Hirayama Seisai}}, and Konosetsu Tsume jointly petitioned the Ministry of Religion for the establishment of a government office for Shinto.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=21-22}}{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=104}}

The next day, March 28, 1875, he{{Who|date=May 2023}} received permission to establish the Bureau of Shinto Affairs.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=21-22}} On April 8, he requested that the Ministry of Religion establish the Bureau of Shinto Affairs. The content of the request was that even small shrines, centering on the Imperial Shrine at Ise, should be able to cooperate with each other for the purpose of propagating Shinto.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=21-22}} On April 15, the Bureau of Shinto Affairs was opened in the Tokyo Branch Office of the Jingu Shichosha.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=105}} Once the Bureau of Shinto Affairs was prepared—bringing together the traditionally existing shrines, Shinto {{Transl|ja|kosha}}, and congregations following folk beliefs—various denominations that met certain conditions were able to branch out and become independent from it. 

The following year, in 1876 (Meiji 9), a {{ill|Dormitory|en|Dormitory|WD=Q847950|lt=Dormitory|1=Dormitory}} was established in the Shinto Office to train priests. Also that year, the [[Kurozumikyō]] and {{ill|Shinto Shusei|en|Shinto Shusei|WD=Q11590921|lt=Shinto Shusei|1=Shintō Shūsei-ha}}, which had been flourishing, became independent denominations.{{Sfn|村上|2007|pp=105-106}}

Inaba Masakuni was the first president of the Bureau of Shinto Affairs.{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=38}} Yoriyasu Tanaka was the Chief of Ise Jingu and the first head of [[Jingūkyō]].{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=33-34}} {{ill|Hirayama Seisai|en|Hirayama Seisai|WD=Q24874598|lt=Hirayama Seisai|1=Hirayama Seisai}} was the grand priest of Hikawa Shrine and the first headmaster of {{ill|Shintō Taiseikyō|en|Shintō Taiseikyō|WD=Q111992480|lt=Shinto Taiseikyo|1=Shintō Taiseikyō}} and [[:en:Ontake-kyo|Ontake-kyo]].{{Sfn|井上順孝ほか編|1996|p=556}} Kousetsu Tsume would become the second head minister of the Ontake Sect.{{Sfn|井上順孝ほか編|1996|p=41}}

In 1886, the Bureau of Shinto Affairs was reorganized, later becoming the sect [[Shintō Taikyō|Shinto Taikyo]].

==== Controversy over shrine deities ====
The Bureau of Shinto Affairs had a plan to make Jingu Haruhaiden (later becoming [[Tokyo Daijingu]]) the central temple{{Sfn|村上|1974|pp=118-119}} and a center for missionary work.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=107}} Since Jingu Haruhaiden was to enshrine a branch spirit of [[Amaterasu]], not only the Ministry of Religion but also the Emperor visited the building and obtained permission from the {{ill|Seiin|ja|正院|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seiin|1=Seiin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545715}} to begin construction, which was funded by donations from the Imperial Household Agency and various families.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=107}}

In 1880, the opinion of [[Senge Takatomi]] on the deities to be worshipped in the Bureau of Shinto Affairs' temples was so controversial that it divided Shinto into the Ise and Izumo factions.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=27-29}} By order of the Meiji Emperor, a great conference on Shinto was held in January 1881 (Meiji 14), attended by 118 people, including all the chief priests of the government buildings and the instructors of the sixth grade and above. However, the issue could not be settled. Thus, it was settled in February by the imperial decision of the Meiji Emperor.{{Sfn|村上|1974|pp=118-119}}

== Separation of ritual and faith ==
In January 1882, the separation of ritual and religion was enacted by the Ministry of Home Affairs through Bill No. 7, which prohibited those in the {{Transl|ja|[[Kyodo Shoku|kyōdō shoku]]}} (priest-teacher position) from performing rituals, thereby promoting the separation of those who continued to be priests performing rituals or preaching the teachings, and solidifying the formation of Sect Shinto.{{Sfn|井上|1991|pp=27-29}}<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />{{Quote frame|Priests shall no longer serve as teachers and shall not be involved in funeral services.|January 24, Meiji 15, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications No. 7}}After this, on May 15, 1882, the six factions (including Jingūkyō) became independent. Jingu Haruhayashiden{{Verify spelling|date=May 2023}} (the source of the ritual god controversy) was transferred to Jingūkyō's ownership and renamed [[Tokyo Daijingu|Daijingu Shrine]], and [[Jingū taima|Jingū Taima]] were distributed by Jingūkyō.{{Sfn|村上|2007|pp=117-118}} [[Senge Takatomi]] took the opportunity to resign from his position as priest of Izumo Taisha Shrine and handed it over to his younger brother, who became the head of the Izumo Taisha Sect.{{Sfn|菅田|1985|pp=149-158}}

On August 11, 1884, the government issued a proclamation abolishing the {{Transl|ja|kyōdō shoku}} position.{{Sfn|村上|2007|pp=120-123}} In turn, this meant the Bureau of Shinto Affairs had lost its original reason for opening,{{Sfn|村上|2007|pp=120-123}} and so in 1886, the Bureau reorganized; it later became [[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinto Taikyo]], one of the schools of Shinto.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

=== Office of Japanese Classics Research ===
{{Main|Office of Japanese Classics Research}}

On November 4, 1881, the [[:en:Office of Japanese Classics Research|Office of Japanese Classics Research]] was established as a successor to the Bureau of Shinto Affairs.{{Sfn|Inoue|1991|p=29}} Like its predecessor, it was a unified Shinto missionary organization established to train Shinto priests.<ref name="a">{{Cite web |last=東京ライフ社刊 |title=皇典講究所から国学院へ |url=http://www.shinto-taikyo.org/shoukai/meiji_130/kouten_kenkyujyo_kara_kokugakuin.htm |access-date=2016-03-16 |publisher=[[神道大教]]}}</ref> Funded by an imperial gift, it purchased a mansion in Iidacho, Kojimachi-ku (present-day {{ill|Chiyoda, Tokyo|en|Chiyoda, Tokyo|WD=Q214051|lt=Chiyoda-ku|1=Chiyoda, Tokyo}}).<ref name="a" />

Immediately after the Great Council of Shinto, it was decided to establish the Office upon the proposal of Akiyoshi Yamada of {{ill|Lord of Home Affairs|ja|内務卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lord of Home Affairs|1=Lord of Home Affairs|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q48743708}}.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=115}} {{ill|Prince Arisugawa Takahito|en|Prince Arisugawa Takahito|WD=Q7243817|lt=Prince Arisugawa Takahito|1=Prince Arisugawa Takahito}} was appointed as its first president, and announced his intention to pursue a unique Japanese academic discipline.<ref>{{Cite web |title=設置の趣旨等を記載した書類 - 大学設置室 - 文部科学省 |url=http://www.dsecchi.mext.go.jp/d_1204t/pdf/kokugakuin_1204tsecchi_syushi1.pdf}}</ref> In the "Announcement of the Establishment of the Imperial Academy" (jointly signed by Li-Kuro Kubo, Yorikuni Inoue, Nakasaburo Itsumi, and Hans Shishino), the intention of the establishment of the academy was to train personnel to maintain {{Transl|ja|[[kokutai]]}} (national identity).{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=115}} The Imperial Institute established branches in the provinces and qualified students for priesthood.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=115}}

The Office was later succeeded by {{ill|Kokugakuin University|en|Kokugakuin University|WD=Q495330|lt=Kokugakuin University|1=Kokugakuin University}}.

=== Academics ===
In December 1868 (the first year of Meiji), the Imperial Academy was established in Kyoto but was abolished the following year. When the Ministry of Religion was established in 1872, it was responsible for research.{{Clarify|reason=What research?|date=May 2023}}{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=114}}

In 1882 (Meiji 15), institutes of imperial studies were established one after another. This was due to a keen awareness of the need for doctrinal studies in the rites and rituals controversy. The controversy was divided between the doctrinalists (denominational Shinto sects) and the national scholars (academics). As the doctrinalists became independent, the national scholars were stimulated and the separation of doctrine and learning progressed.{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=29}} On April 30, Jingūkyō established {{ill|Kogakkan University|en|Kogakkan University|WD=Q1797584|lt=Kōgakkan University|1=Kogakkan University}} in Ise.{{Sfn|井上|1991|p=29}} On May 30, the Department of Classics was established at the {{ill|University of Tokyo|en|University of Tokyo|WD=Q7842|lt=University of Tokyo|1=University of Tokyo}}.{{Sfn|村上|2007|p=115}}

== After World War II ==
{{Main|Shinto Directive}}

On December 15, 1945, the [[Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers]] (GHQ) issued the [[Shinto Directive]] aimed at dismantling State Shinto. In January of the following year, the Dai Nihon Shinto-kai, the Imperial Academy, and the Jingu Bonan-kai were dissolved to form the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]], a religious corporation.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=231}} In March, Jingu-Shogakukan University was abolished by the Shinto directive; in April, representatives of each denomination explained their denomination to the GHQ Civilian Information and Education Department at Broadcasting Hall 108.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=228}} In June, at a meeting at Tenrikyo's Honshiba Grand Church between the presidents of the various schools and W. K. Vance, head of the Religious Affairs Division at GHQ, the occupying forces promised not to impose any restrictions on the religious activities of the Shinto sects.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=228}}

Tenrikyo established a policy of restoration immediately in 1945, and Konkokyo established the Council for the Establishment of the Faith in 1951 to eliminate Shinto colors.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=229}}

The system in which there were 13 Shinto sects and 13 Buddhist sects recognized by the government was broken up into even smaller groups as religious organizations when the Religious Corporation Law was enacted.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

=== Shinto research institutions ===
Many of the scholars who had played a central role in Shinto research and education were expelled and replaced by folklorists such as {{ill|Shinobu Orikuchi|en|Shinobu Orikuchi|WD=Q3482286|lt=Shinobu Orikuchi|1=Shinobu Orikuchi}} and [[Kunio Yanagita]], as well as younger Shinto scholars who escaped expulsion.{{Sfn|中山|2009|pp=231-232}} On March 20, 1946, {{ill|Kokugakuin University|en|Kokugakuin University|WD=Q495330|lt=Kokugakuin University|1=Kokugakuin University}} became a corporation, and the training of priests, which had been commissioned by the Ministry of Home Affairs, was continued from April as a new commission from the Jinja Main Office. The following year, Vance and Woodard of the Religious Affairs Division of GHQ decided that there was no problem with the study of Shinto and training of priests as a private university, and in 1948, the Shinto Affairs Department was established to form a Shinto training organization.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=232}}

The [[:en:Shinto Scholarship Association|Shinto Scholarship Association]], which had been conducting Shinto courses, was also dissolved in 1946.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=238}} In July 1949, at a meeting of the Federation of Shinto Sects at the Kinko Grand Church of the Tenrikyo Tokyo Branch Office, it was decided that Shinto lectures would be held at the Shinto Training Department of Kokugakuin University on behalf of the Federation of Shinto Sects; this practice continued until 1966.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=238}} Holding the Shinto course promoted the university as a Shinto university that combined both Shrine Shinto and Sect Shinto.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=238}} As of 1996, Kokugakuin University was said to be the only university with a course on Sect Shinto.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

== Sects ==

== Overview ==
There are five main groups of Sect Shinto:<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

# [[Fukko Shinto]] (Revival Shinto) lineage – includes [[Shintō Taikyō|Shinto Taikyo]], [[Shinrikyo]], and [[Izumo-taishakyo]] (which originates from [[Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]])<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />
# [[Confucian Shinto]] – {{Nihongo|[[:en:Shinto Taiseikyo|Shinto Taiseikyo]]|神道大成教}} and {{ill|Shinto Shusei|en|Shinto Shusei|WD=Q11590921|lt=Shinto Shusei|1=Shintō Shūsei-ha}}<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />
# {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}} lineage – includes [[Jikkō kyō]], [[Fuso-kyo]], and [[:en:Ontake-kyo|Ontake-kyo]]<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />
# Purification sects – [[Misogikyo]] and [[Shinshu-kyo]]<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />
# Utopian groups – [[Kurozumikyō]], [[Tenrikyo]], and {{ill|Konkokyo|en|Konkokyo|WD=Q897040|lt=Konkokyo|1=Konkokyo}}<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

Tenrikyo is now classified by the Agency for Cultural Affairs as one of the various religions, not as a Shinto denomination.{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=5-6}}

=== History ===
The first independent denominations were [[Kurozumikyō]] and {{ill|Shinto Shusei|en|Shinto Shusei|WD=Q11590921|lt=Shinto Shusei|1=Shintō Shūsei-ha}} in 1876 (Meiji 9). [[Jingūkyō]] was founded in 1882, but later reorganized into the Ise Shrine Offering Association{{Efn|This was one of the predecessor organizations that formed the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]] after World War II.}}{{Needs independent confirmation|reason=This name's translation needs to be confirmed. The Wikipedia page for Jingukyo gives the name as "Jingū Service Foundation".|date=May 2023}} in 1899 (Meiji 32).<ref name="戦後に神社本庁を形成する前身組織の1つ-2">戦後に[[神社本庁]]を形成する前身組織の1つ。</ref> 

In 1895, eight denominations—[[Izumo-taishakyo|Izumo Taisha-kyo]], [[Kurozumikyō]], {{ill|Ontake-kyō|en|Ontake-kyō|WD=Q6880734|lt=Ontake-kyo|1=Ontake-kyō}}, [[Jikkō kyō]], [[:en:Shinto Taiseikyo|Shinto Taiseikyo]], [[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinshu-kyo]], [[Fuso-kyo]], and [[Jingūkyō]]—joined to form the {{Transl|ja|Shintō Dōshikai}} ({{Lit|Society of Shinto Colleagues}}).<ref name="tudoi2">Inori and Tsudoi: A History of the 100th Anniversary of the Formation of the Shinto Federation of Churches, 1996, pp. 10-12.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |year=2001 |title=Kyôha Shintô Rengôkai 教派神道連合会 |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/index2.html |access-date=2023-05-16 |website=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms |publisher=Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics, Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref name="nobutaka-2023b">{{Cite web |last=Nobutaka |first=Inoue |title=Encyclopedia of Shinto 詳細 - 8. Schools, Groups, and Personalities - Kyōha Shintō Rengōkai |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp//eos/detail/ |access-date=2023-05-16 |publisher={{ill|Kokugakuin University|en|Kokugakuin University|WD=Q495330|lt=Kokugakuin University|1=Kokugakuin University}}}}</ref> In 1899 (Meiji 32), the group was joined by Shinto Headquarters ([[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinto Taikyo]]), [[Shinrikyo]], and [[Misogikyo]], and the name was changed to {{Transl|ja|Shintō Konwakai}}; the same year, Jingūkyō reorganized as Jingū Hōnsaikai and withdrew from the federation.<ref name="nobutaka-2023b" /> In 1912 (Meiji 45), {{ill|Konkokyo|en|Konkokyo|WD=Q897040|lt=Konkokyo|1=Konkokyo}}, {{ill|Shinto Shusei|en|Shinto Shusei|WD=Q11590921|lt=Shinto Shusei|1=Shintō Shūsei-ha}}, and [[Tenrikyo]] joined, forming 13 groups (14 if including the breakaway Jingūkyō), and the name was changed to {{Transl|ja| Shintō Kyōha Rengōkai}}.<ref name="tudoi2" /> In 1934, the current name {{Nihongo3|Federation of Sectarian Shinto|教派神道連合会|Kyōha Shintō Rengōkai}} was adopted.<ref name="tudoi2" />

After World War II, [[Oomoto]] joined the federation, but [[Tenrikyo]] and {{ill|Shintō Taiseikyō|en|Shintō Taiseikyō|WD=Q111992480|lt=Shinto Taiseikyo|1=Shintō Taiseikyō}} withdrew. [[Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto]] was re-established after the war, but never joined the federation. Shinshu-kyo withdrew in 1959 but returned in 1994.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

In 1995, on the occasion of the 100th anniversary of its formation, the "100th Anniversary of the Formation of the Federation of Shinto Churches" was held.<ref name="100ani">{{Cite news |date=1995-09-05 |script-title=ja:結成100周年の記念式典 |script-work=ja:産経新聞}}</ref> In addition to Misogi-kyo, Shinto Taikyo, Jingūkyō, Konkokyo, Kurozumikyō, Fuso-kyo, Ontake-kyo, Shinrikyo, Oomoto, Shinshu-kyo, Shinto Shusei, Izumo Taisha-kyo, and twelve other denominations, the presidents of Tenrikyo and [[:en:Shinto Taiseikyo|Shinto Taiseikyo]] also attended.<ref name="100ani" />

Today, the federation has 12 affiliated groups.<ref name="nobutaka-2023b" />

=== Kurozumikyō ===
{{Main|Kurozumikyō}}
Kurozumikyō (黒住教) is a group highly linked to [[Amaterasu]].

=== Shinto Shusei ===
{{nihongo|Shinto Shusei|神道修成派}} is considered a form of [[Confucian Shinto]].{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=5-6}}<ref name="caroline-myss-2023a">{{Cite web |title=The Forms of Shinto |url=https://www.myss.com/free-resources/world-religions/shinto/the-forms-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-03-06 |website=Caroline Myss |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" /> It was founded in 1849 by {{ill|Nitta Kuniteru|en|Nitta Kuniteru|WD=Q123561044|lt=Nitta Kuniteru|1=Nitta Kuniteru}} (1829–1902),<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> who was known to have read the {{ill|Analects|en|Analects|WD=Q276015|lt=Analects|1=Analects}} at age 9.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> He founded the sect at age twenty,<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> and considered Japanese people to be descendants of deities.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" /> He considered allegiance to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}} to be central to his philosophy; he was a supporter of [[Sonnō jōi]] but supported the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin Rebellion|1=Boshin War}} and the [[Meiji Restoration]] later.<ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム" />

Alongside [[Kurozumikyō]], it was one of the first two Shinto sects to gain independence in 1876.<ref name="戦後に神社本庁を形成する前身組織の1つ-2" /> It has not been very active in the postwar era.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2001 |title=Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms - Shintô shûsei-ha 神道修成派 |url=https://archive.today/20230321180610/https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_S.html |publisher=Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics, Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

=== Jingūkyō ===
{{Main|Jingūkyō}}
{{Nihongo|Jingūkyō|神宮教}} was a sect run out of [[Ise Grand Shrine]] which distributed [[Jingū taima|Jingu Taima]]. It was a rival to [[Izumo-taishakyo]] and eventually left the federation and came to dominate {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}.

=== Izumo-taishakyo ===
{{Main|Izumo-taishakyo}}
Izumo-taishakyo was founded by [[Senge Takatomi]].<ref name="google3"/><ref>{{cite book |author1=Teeuwen, M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yBFFAz4z3gUC |title=Shinto, a Short History |author2=Breen, J. |author3=Inoue, N. |author4=Mori, M. |date=2003 |publisher=RoutledgeCurzon |isbn=9780415311793 |page=177 |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref>  and has 1,266,058 followers.<ref name="Religious Almanac" /> It is a [[Fukko Shinto]] lineage and at one point was a major rival with [[Jingūkyō]].

=== Fuso-kyo ===
{{nihongo|Fusō-kyō|扶桑教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}} sect traditionally seen to have been founded by {{ill|Hasegawa Kakugyo|en|Hasegawa Kakugyo|WD=Q11630860|lt=Hasegawa Kakugyo|1=Hasegawa Kakugyo}} (who was also associated with Jikkō kyō).<ref name="picken-2010a">{{Cite book |last=Picken |first=Stuart D. B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&dq=Jikk%C5%8D+ky%C5%8D&pg=PA131 |title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto |date=2010-12-28 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0-8108-7372-8 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Jikkō kyō ===
{{nihongo|Jikkō kyō|実行教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}} sect traditionally seen to have been founded by {{ill|Hasegawa Kakugyo|en|Hasegawa Kakugyo|WD=Q11630860|lt=Hasegawa Kakugyo|1=Hasegawa Kakugyo}} (who was also associated with Fusō-kyō).<ref name="picken-2010a" />

=== Shinto Taiseikyo ===
{{Main|Shinto Taiseikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Shinto Taiseikyo|神道大成教}} is a [[Confucian Shinto]] sect<ref name="caroline-myss-2023a"/><ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" /> founded by {{ill|Hirayama Seisai|en|Hirayama Seisai|WD=Q24874598|lt=Hirayama Seisai|1=Hirayama Seisai}}.

=== Shinshu-kyo ===
{{Nihongo|Shinshu-kyo|神習教}} is a "purification sect" alongside [[Misogikyo]].<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

It was founded by Masaki Yoshimura<ref>{{Cite web |last=小項目事典 |first=朝日日本歴史人物事典,デジタル版 日本人名大辞典+Plus,ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 |title=芳村正秉(よしむら・まさもち)とは？ 意味や使い方 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%8A%B3%E6%9D%91%E6%AD%A3%E7%A7%89-146230 |access-date=2023-03-06 |website=コトバンク |language=ja}}</ref> (1839–1915<ref>{{Cite web |title=歴史 |url=http://shinshukyo.jp/%e6%ad%b4%e5%8f%b2/ |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=神道神習教公式ページ |language=ja}}</ref>), who was a survivor of the {{ill|Ansei Purge|en|Ansei Purge|WD=Q569487|lt=Ansei Purge|1=Ansei Purge}}.{{sfn|井上順孝|1991|p=277-278}} He worked at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]] and later was head of [[Tatsuta Taisha|Tatsuta Shrine]], but due to laws restricting teaching, he entrusted his children to [[Itō Hirobumi]] (before he became Prime Minister) and established a new branch based on his {{ill|family knowledge|ja|家学|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/family knowledge|qq=}}.{{sfn|井上順孝|1991|p=282}}

=== Ontake-kyo ===
{{Main|Ontake-kyo}}
{{Nihongo|Ontake-kyo|御嶽教}} is a {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}} sect dedicated to {{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake|WD=Q1754806|lt=Mount Ontake|1=Mount Ontake}}.<ref>{{cite book |author=Holtom, D.C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=znzXAAAAMAAJ |title=The National Faith of Japan: A Study in Modern Shinto |date=1938 |publisher=Paragon Book Reprint Corporation |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> It had 3 million members in 1930,<ref name="googlebooks">{{cite book |author=Picken, S.D.B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yA3_11C6pPgC |title=Essentials of Shinto: An Analytical Guide to Principal Teachings |date=1994 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=9780313264313 |page=232 |access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> which decreased to around 40,000 members in 2020.<ref name="Religious Almanac" />

=== Shinto Taikyo ===
{{Main|Shinto Taikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Shintō Taikyō|神道大教}} is the direct successor to the [[Taikyo Institute]]. Its name "Taikyo" refers to the [[:en:Three Great Teachings|Three Great Teachings]] first proclaimed in the [[Taikyo Proclamation|Proclamation of the Great Doctrine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shinto Taikyo |url=http://www.philtar.ac.uk/encyclopedia/shinto/shitai.html |access-date=2023-03-12 |website=www.philtar.ac.uk}}</ref>

=== Shinrikyo ===
{{nihongo|Shinrikyo|神理教|4={{lit|divine principle}}}} is a Shinto sect considered to be part of the [[Fukko Shinto]] lineage of Sect Shinto, alongside [[:en:Shinto Taikyo|Shinto Taikyo]] and [[Izumo-taishakyo]].{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=5-6}} The name "Shinrikyo" is relatively common among Shinto groups,<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> and uses different {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji|1=Kanji}} characters than {{ill|Aum Shinrikyo|en|Aum Shinrikyo|WD=Q217408|lt=Aum Shinrikyo|1=Aum Shinrikyo}}, a cult and terrorist organization.

It was founded by {{ill|Tsunehiko Sano|ja|佐野経彦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunehiko Sano|1=Tsunehiko Sano|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11385093}}<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp">{{Cite web |title=Sano Tsunehiko and "Divine Principle (Shinri)" |url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/cpjr/kami/inoue.html |access-date=2023-03-05 |website=www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref><ref name="日本国語大辞典,百科事典マイペディア,デジタル大辞泉,世界大百科事典内言及" /> in 1880.<ref name="notes-1989a" /><ref name="日本国語大辞典,百科事典マイペディア,デジタル大辞泉,世界大百科事典内言及" /> Sano had previously studied medicine and was an advocate of traditional Japanese medicine. He studied {{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku|1=Kokugaku}} in his youth under Nishida Naokai.<ref>https://rks.accesson.kr/assets/pdf/2564/journal-23-1-211.pdf {{Bare URL PDF|date=August 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp//eos/detail/id=9473|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム}}</ref>

Sano's thought blurred the lines between monotheism and polytheism, entering {{ill|Transtheism|en|Transtheism|WD=Q312221|lt=Transtheism|1=Transtheism}}.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> His concept of {{Transl|ja|[[kami]]}} was aimed at resisting the propagation of Christianity while composing teachings that were in line with the aims of popular national indoctrination. His core elements of the concept of {{Transl|ja|kami}} did not change throughout his life.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" />

He believed the etymology of {{Transl|ja|kami}} was derived from {{Nihongo|vital force||Ikimochi}}. He saw this as emphasizing the interconnectedness of everything, from humans to nature, and as such this could be interpreted as a monotheistic view.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" /> He saw all the {{Transl|ja|kami}} as unified under a divine principle, hence the name of the group.<ref name="www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp" />

=== Misogikyo ===
{{nihongo|Misogikyo|禊教|4={{lit|[[Misogi]] religion}}}} is considered a "purification sect" alongside [[Shinshu-kyo]].<ref name="Encyclopedia Britannica" />

The group is quite obscure today.<ref name="sawada-1998a">{{Cite journal |last=Sawada |first=Janine Anderson |date=1998 |title=Mind and Morality in Nineteenth-Century Japanese Religions: Misogi-Kyō and Maruyama-Kyō |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1399927 |journal=Philosophy East and West |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=108–141 |doi=10.2307/1399927 |jstor=1399927 |issn=0031-8221}}</ref> It is very ritual-focused, with little theoretical theology. In this way, it contrasts with [[:en:Yoshida Shinto|Yoshida Shinto]].<ref name="sawada-1998a" /> It emphasizes right state of mind and self-control.<ref name="sawada-1998a" /> It has influence from [[Confucian Shinto]] but is its own tradition.<ref name="sawada-1998a" />

=== Konkokyo ===
{{Main|Konkokyo}}
{{Nihongo|Konkōkyō|金光教|Konkō-kyō}} is a group often considered to be its own religion, which emerged from [[Shinbutsu-shūgō]].

=== Tenrikyo ===
{{Main|Tenrikyo}}
{{Nihongo|Tenrikyo||Tenrikyō|sometimes rendered as 'Tenriism'}} is a Sect Shinto group founded by {{ill|Nakayama Miki|en|Nakayama Miki|WD=Q2723199|lt=Nakayama Miki|1=Nakayama Miki}}. It is often considered a separate religion from Shinto.

=== Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto ===
{{Main|Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto}}
In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, the Tsuchimikado family, descendants of [[Abe no Seimei]], established [[Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto]] influenced by [[Confucian Shinto]] through [[Suika Shinto]]. However, because of the inclusion of fortune-telling and magic, the Meiji government considered it pagan and issued the {{interlanguage link|Tensha Shinto Prohibition Ordinance|ja|天社禁止令|1=Tensha Shinto Prohibition Ordinance}}. After the war, it was restored as "Tensha Tsuchimikado Shinto Headquarters", and registered as a [[religious corporation]] rather than a Sect Shinto or a Shinto shrine.{{Citation needed|date=April 2022}}

=== Oomoto ===
{{Main|Oomoto}}
{{Nihongo|Oomoto|大本|Ōmoto|{{lit|Great Source, or Great Origin}}}} is often seen as a new religion.

=== New Sect Shinto ===
{{See also|Japanese new religions}}
{{Nihongo|New Sect Shinto||shin kyoha Shinto}}<ref name="google2">{{cite book|title=Excel Senior High School Studies of Religion|author=Fleming, L.|date=2001|publisher=Pascal Press |isbn=9781740202411 |url={{Google books |plainurl=yes |id=Q_K81HQFoyoC }} |page=278|access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> is a subset of Sect Shinto,<ref name="jinja">{{cite web|url=http://jinja.jp/english/s-2.html|title=Shuha Shinto|publisher=jinja.jp|access-date=2015-01-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150101161525/http://jinja.jp/english/s-2.html|archive-date=2015-01-01|url-status=dead}}</ref> and consists of numerous organizations.<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=World Christian Trends, AD 30-AD 2200: Interpreting the Annual Christian Megacensus|author1=Barrett, D.B.|author2=Johnson, T.M.|author3=Guidry, C.R.|author4=Crossing, P.F.|date=2001|issue=Bd. 1|publisher=William Carey Library|isbn=9780878086085 |url={{Google books |plainurl=yes |id=IMRsJ1gnIYkC }} |page=606|access-date=2015-01-01}}</ref> It is influenced by {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}} and {{ill|Confucianism|en|Confucianism|WD=Q9581|lt=Confucianism|1=Confucianism}}.<ref name="jinja" />

It is part of the Sect Shinto movement not centering upon 13 sects.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003">{{cite journal | citeseerx=10.1.1.567.8041 | title=Intercultural Communication Studies XII-4 2003 Asian Approaches to Human Communication Aspects of Shinto in Japanese Communication }}</ref> New Shinto sects have {{ill|Shamanism|en|Shamanism|WD=Q42042|lt=shamanistic|1=Shamanism}} leadership, syncretism of religious and philosophical beliefs, closely knit social organization, and individualism.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003"/> Some groups have characteristics of {{ill|Monotheism|en|Monotheism|WD=Q9159|lt=Monotheism|1=Monotheism}}, in the extreme case making a compromise of {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}, {{ill|Confucianism|en|Confucianism|WD=Q9581|lt=Confucianism|1=Confucianism}}, and {{ill|Folk religion|en|Folk religion|WD=Q1068640|lt=Folk religion|1=Folk religion}}.<ref name="ICS xii-4 2003"/>
